cards.english: Definite articles: der / die / das
cards.grammarNote:
Every German noun has a gender: **masculine** (der), **feminine** (die), or **neuter** (das).
Gender must be memorized with each noun — there is no universal rule.
The definite article also changes with case, so knowing gender is essential.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee / the milk / the bread
cards.phrase: der Kaffee / die Milch / das Brot

table.title: Definite Articles — Nominative
table.note: Learn every noun with its article: der Kaffee, die Milch, das Brot.

cards.english: Indefinite articles: ein / eine / ein
cards.grammarNote:
Use **ein** (m/n) or **eine** (f) for 'a / an'.
**ein Kaffee** (m), **eine Banane** (f), **ein Ei** (n).
Feminine is the only gender that changes — masculine and neuter both use *ein*.
cards.englishPhrase: A coffee, a banana, an egg
cards.phrase: ein Kaffee, eine Banane, ein Ei

table.title: Indefinite Articles — Nominative
table.note: Only feminine changes: ein → eine.

cards.english: Plural formation — common patterns
cards.grammarNote:
German plurals follow several patterns — always check a dictionary.
The definite article for ALL plurals is **die**, regardless of gender.
Common endings: -e, -(e)n, -er, -s, and umlaut (Umlaut + ending).
cards.englishPhrase: the books, the bananas, the eggs, the cars, the apples
cards.phrase: die Bücher, die Bananen, die Eier, die Autos, die Äpfel

table.title: Plural Patterns (common)
table.note: All plurals use die. Learn plural with each noun.

cards.english: Personal pronouns — nominative (subject)
cards.word: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie
cards.grammarNote:
These are the subject pronouns — use them as the doer of the action.
**Sie** (capital S) is the formal 'you' (singular and plural).
**sie** (lowercase) means 'she' (sg) or 'they' (pl) — context tells them apart.
cards.englishPhrase: I, you, he, she, it, we, you all, they, you (formal)
cards.phrase: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie

table.title: Personal Pronouns — Nominative
table.note: Sie (formal) is always capitalised.

cards.english: sein — to be (present tense)
cards.grammarNote:
**sein** is highly irregular — every form must be memorized.
Use it for identity, origin, states: *Ich bin müde.* *Er ist Arzt.*
Note: *Sie sind* covers both 'they are' and formal 'you are'.
cards.englishPhrase: I am tired. She is a nurse. We are happy.
cards.phrase: Ich bin müde. Sie ist Krankenschwester. Wir sind glücklich.

table.title: sein — present tense
table.note: Irregular — memorise all forms.

cards.english: haben — to have (present tense)
cards.grammarNote:
**haben** is also slightly irregular: *du hast*, *er hat* (no -b-).
Used for possession and many fixed expressions: *Ich habe Hunger* (I'm hungry).
Also the auxiliary for many past tenses.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a coffee. Do you have the bill? He has patience.
cards.phrase: Ich habe einen Kaffee. Hast du die Rechnung? Er hat Geduld.

table.title: haben — present tense
table.note: du hast / er hat — the -b- drops.

cards.english: Regular present-tense endings (e.g. spielen)
cards.grammarNote:
Drop the **-en** infinitive ending to get the stem, then add the personal ending.
Stem of *spielen* = *spiel-* → **ich spiele**, **du spielst**, **er spielt**…
These endings apply to nearly all regular verbs.
cards.englishPhrase: I play, you play, he plays, we play, you all play, they play
cards.phrase: ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen

table.title: Regular endings — spielen (to play)
table.note: Stem = infinitive minus -en. Add the ending.

cards.english: Stems ending in -t or -d: extra -e- before -st / -t (e.g. arbeiten)
cards.grammarNote:
When the stem ends in **-t** or **-d**, add **-e-** before *-st* and *-t* endings.
*arbeit-* → **du arbeitest**, **er arbeitet** (not *arbeitst* / *arbeitt*).
This keeps the word pronounceable. Same rule applies to *reden*, *warten*, etc.
cards.englishPhrase: You work at the office. He works every day.
cards.phrase: Du arbeitest im Büro. Er arbeitet jeden Tag.

cloze.prompt: She works at the office (arbeiten, er/sie/es form)

cards.english: The V2 rule — conjugated verb is always the 2nd element
cards.grammarNote:
In a German main clause the **conjugated verb is always in position 2**, regardless of what starts the sentence.
If an adverb or phrase comes first (position 1), the subject shifts to position 3.
*Heute **trinke** ich Kaffee.* — verb stays second.
cards.englishPhrase: Today I drink coffee. (verb stays 2nd even when 'today' is first)
cards.phrase: Heute trinke ich Kaffee.

contrast.prompt: Normal order vs. adverb-first — verb position?

b.gloss: Adverb first — subject shifts, verb still 2nd

cards.english: Yes/no questions — verb moves to position 1
cards.grammarNote:
For yes/no questions, put the **conjugated verb first** — the subject follows immediately.
There is no equivalent of English 'do/does': *Trinkst du Tee?* = 'Do you drink tea?'
Statement word order simply inverts: Subject–Verb → Verb–Subject.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you drink tea? Do you work today?
cards.phrase: Trinkst du Tee? Arbeitest du heute?

cards.english: W-questions — question word + conjugated verb + subject
cards.word: wer / was / wo / wann / warum / wie
cards.grammarNote:
W-question words take **position 1**; the verb comes second (V2 rule still applies).
*Wo **ist** das Restaurant?* / *Was **trinkst** du?*
The question word itself counts as element 1.
cards.englishPhrase: Where is the restaurant? What are you drinking? When does the train come?
cards.phrase: Wo ist das Restaurant? Was trinkst du? Wann kommt der Zug?

table.title: W-question words
table.note: W-word is position 1; verb is position 2.

cards.english: Negation with nicht — negating verbs and adjectives
cards.grammarNote:
**nicht** negates verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
It usually comes after the conjugated verb and its object, but **before** adjectives/past participles.
*Ich trinke **nicht** Kaffee.* / *Er ist **nicht** müde.*
cards.englishPhrase: I don't drink coffee. He is not tired.
cards.phrase: Ich trinke nicht Kaffee. Er ist nicht müde.

produce.concept: Place nicht after the conjugated verb (and object if there is one).
produce.task: Negate: 'Sie singt.' and 'Das Essen ist lecker.'
produce.answer: Sie singt nicht. / Das Essen ist nicht lecker.
produce.gloss: nicht follows the verb (singt) or precedes the predicate adjective (lecker)

cards.english: Negation with kein/keine — negating nouns
cards.grammarNote:
Use **kein/keine** (not *nicht ein*) to negate a noun — it follows the *ein*-pattern.
*Ich habe **keinen** Kaffee.* (m-acc) / *Ich habe **keine** Milch.* (f)
Quick rule: where you'd say *ein/eine*, negate it with *kein/keine*.
cards.englishPhrase: I have no coffee. She has no milk. There is no bread.
cards.phrase: Ich habe keinen Kaffee. Sie hat keine Milch. Es gibt kein Brot.

contrast.prompt: nicht vs. kein — which do you use?

cards.english: möchten — would like (present tense)
cards.grammarNote:
**möchten** is a modal-like verb meaning 'would like' — very polite and common.
Note: *er/sie/es möchte* has **no** -t ending (unlike regular verbs).
Always followed by an infinitive or a noun: *Ich möchte Tee trinken.*
cards.englishPhrase: I would like a tea. She would like to travel.
cards.phrase: Ich möchte einen Tee. Sie möchte reisen.

table.title: möchten — present tense
table.note: er/sie/es möchte — no extra -t.

cards.english: Formal vs. informal address: du vs. Sie
cards.grammarNote:
Use **du** with friends, family, children, and peers.
Use **Sie** (always capitalised) with strangers, officials, and in professional settings.
*Sie* takes the same verb form as 3rd-person plural: *Sie trinken* = 'you (formal) drink'.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you speak English? (formal) vs. Do you speak English? (informal)
cards.phrase: Sprechen Sie Englisch? vs. Sprichst du Englisch?

contrast.prompt: Talking to a stranger (formal) vs. a friend (informal)

cards.english: Subject-verb inversion when an adverb or phrase starts the sentence
cards.grammarNote:
When anything other than the subject is in **position 1**, the subject and verb invert.
*Heute* (pos 1) + *esse* (verb, pos 2) + *ich* (subject, pos 3).
This is the V2 rule in action — the verb never leaves position 2.
cards.englishPhrase: Today I eat pasta. Tomorrow she is at the café.
cards.phrase: Heute esse ich Nudeln. Morgen ist sie im Café.

cloze.prompt: Start with 'Heute' (today) — invert subject and verb: 'Today I am tired'

cards.english: Accusative preview: der → den for masculine direct objects
cards.grammarNote:
The **direct object** (accusative) changes the masculine article: **der → den**.
Feminine (*die*), neuter (*das*), and plural (*die*) stay the same in accusative.
*Ich esse **den** Apfel.* — der Apfel is now the object, so it becomes *den Apfel*.
cards.englishPhrase: The apple is on the table. I am eating the apple.
cards.phrase: Der Apfel liegt auf dem Tisch. Ich esse den Apfel.

contrast.prompt: der Apfel as subject (nominative) vs. direct object (accusative)

cards.english: es gibt — there is / there are
cards.grammarNote:
**es gibt** is the standard way to say 'there is/are' — it is always singular (*gibt*).
The noun after *es gibt* is in the **accusative** case.
*Es gibt **einen** Park hier.* (m-acc) / *Es gibt **keine** Haltestelle.* (f)
cards.englishPhrase: There is a park here. There are no buses.
cards.phrase: Es gibt einen Park hier. Es gibt keine Busse.

produce.concept: es gibt + accusative noun = there is/are
produce.task: How do you say 'There is a café here'? (das Café)
produce.gloss: das Café is neuter → accusative is also ein Café (neuter unchanged)

cards.english: Coordinating conjunctions: und (and) / aber (but)
cards.grammarNote:
**und** and **aber** join two clauses with **no change to word order** — the verb stays in position 2 of each clause.
*Ich trinke Kaffee, **aber** er trinkt Tee.*
Both conjunctions are 'zero-position' words: they don't count as element 1.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm hungry and I'm eating soup. I like coffee, but I'm drinking tea.
cards.phrase: Ich habe Hunger und ich esse Suppe. Ich mag Kaffee, aber ich trinke Tee.

contrast.prompt: und (and) vs. aber (but) — both keep V2 in the second clause

a.term: Ich esse Suppe und ich trinke Wasser.

b.term: Ich mag Suppe, aber ich esse Salat.

cards.english: gern — expressing that you like doing something
cards.grammarNote:
Add **gern** after a verb to say you like doing it: *Ich singe **gern**.* = 'I like to sing.'
The opposite is **nicht gern**: *Er isst **nicht gern** Fisch.* = 'He doesn't like eating fish.'
*gern* is an adverb — it does not change form.
cards.englishPhrase: I like to swim. She likes to travel. He doesn't like to cook.
cards.phrase: Ich schwimme gern. Sie reist gern. Er kocht nicht gern.
literal: I swim gladly = I like swimming

cloze.prompt: Say 'I like to read' using gern (lesen = irregular: ich lese)

cards.english: Stem-vowel changes in du/er/sie/es: e→i and e→ie (strong verbs)
cards.grammarNote:
Some strong verbs change their stem vowel in **du** and **er/sie/es** forms only.
**e → i**: *sprechen* → **du sprichst, er spricht**
**e → ie**: *lesen* → **du liest, er liest**
wir/sie forms revert to the normal stem.
cards.englishPhrase: You speak German. He reads the menu.
cards.phrase: Du sprichst Deutsch. Er liest die Speisekarte.

table.title: Stem-vowel changes (e→i / e→ie)
table.note: Only du and er/sie/es change; wir/sie keep the original stem.

cards.english: Sentence bracket (Satzklammer): modal + infinitive at the end
cards.grammarNote:
When a modal verb (*können, möchten*…) is used, it occupies **position 2** and the infinitive goes to the **very end** — creating a bracket around the rest.
*Ich **möchte** heute Kaffee **trinken**.* (modal → pos 2, infinitive → end)
This bracket is fundamental to German sentence structure.
cards.englishPhrase: I would like to drink coffee today. Can you help me?
cards.phrase: Ich möchte heute Kaffee trinken. Kannst du mir helfen?

cloze.prompt: Complete the bracket: 'She would like to learn German.' (möchten + lernen)

cards.english: Indefinite article in accusative: ein → einen (masculine only)
cards.grammarNote:
Just like *der → den*, the indefinite article changes for masculine direct objects: **ein → einen**.
*Ich möchte **einen** Kaffee.* — Kaffee is masculine (der Kaffee) and is the object.
Feminine (*eine*) and neuter (*ein*) stay the same in accusative.
cards.englishPhrase: I would like a coffee (m). I see a banana (f). I'm eating an egg (n).
cards.phrase: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. Ich sehe eine Banane. Ich esse ein Ei.

table.title: Indefinite articles — accusative
table.note: Only masculine changes: ein → einen.

cards.english: Essential everyday questions using pool phrases
cards.grammarNote:
These three question patterns cover most beginner conversations.
**Wie viel kostet…?** = How much does … cost? (verb *kosten*, no movement needed)
**Wo ist…?** / **Was ist…?** follow the same V2 pattern: W-word + verb + subject.
cards.englishPhrase: How much does the coffee cost? Where is the bakery? What is the job?
cards.phrase: Wie viel kostet der Kaffee? Wo ist die Bäckerei? Was ist der Beruf?

produce.concept: W-word + verb (pos 2) + rest of sentence
produce.task: Ask 'Where is the train station?' and 'How much does the ticket cost?'
produce.answer: Wo ist der Bahnhof? / Wie viel kostet die Fahrkarte?
produce.gloss: der Bahnhof (m), die Fahrkarte (f) — articles stay nominative after ist/kostet

cards.english: Regular present-tense endings: spielen paradigm
cards.grammarNote:
Regular verbs follow: **-e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en**.
Remove the infinitive -en to get the stem (spiel-), then add the ending.
This pattern covers the vast majority of German verbs.
cards.englishPhrase: I play, you play, he plays — we play, you play, they play.
cards.phrase: Ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt — wir spielen, ihr spielt, sie spielen.

table.title: spielen — Präsens (regular)
table.note: Ending pattern: -e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en

cards.english: Fill the blank: 'She learns German every day.' — regular present
cards.grammarNote:
**lernen** is fully regular: stem lern- + endings -e/-st/-t/-en/-t/-en.
The er/sie/es form is always stem + **-t**.
So sie (she) → **lernt**.
cards.englishPhrase: She learns German every day.
cards.phrase: Sie lernt jeden Tag Deutsch.

cloze.prompt: She learns German every day. (regular present, er/sie/es form of lernen)

cards.english: Stems ending in -t or -d: insert -e- before the ending (arbeiten)
cards.grammarNote:
When a stem ends in **-t** or **-d**, insert an extra **-e-** before -st and -t endings.
This keeps the word pronounceable: arbeit- → du arbeit**e**st, er arbeit**e**t.
wir/ihr/sie follow the same rule: ihr arbeit**e**t.
cards.englishPhrase: You work in an office; he works in a café.
cards.phrase: Du arbeitest im Büro; er arbeitet im Café.

table.title: arbeiten — Präsens (stem ends in -t)
table.note: Extra -e- inserted before -st and -t endings. Same rule applies to stem-final -d.

cards.english: Stems ending in -s, -ß, or -z: du form takes only -t, not -st
cards.grammarNote:
When the stem ends in **-s**, **-ß**, or **-z**, du already has an s-sound, so the ending is just **-t** (not -st).
heißen: du hei**ßt** (not heißst). tanzen: du tan**zt** (not tanzst).
All other persons follow the regular pattern.
cards.englishPhrase: What is your name? — My name is Anna. / You dance very well.
cards.phrase: Wie heißt du? — Ich heiße Anna. / Du tanzt sehr gut.

table.title: heißen · tanzen — du form
table.note: du adds only -t when stem ends in -s/-ß/-z

cards.english: sein (to be) — full present-tense paradigm
cards.grammarNote:
**sein** is highly irregular — the forms share almost no stem.
Memorize: **bin / bist / ist / sind / seid / sind**.
This verb is needed in almost every German sentence.
cards.englishPhrase: I am tired. You are at home. We are happy.
cards.phrase: Ich bin müde. Du bist zu Hause. Wir sind glücklich.

table.title: sein — Präsens
table.note: Fully irregular — must be memorized.

cards.english: haben (to have) — full present-tense paradigm
cards.grammarNote:
**haben** is irregular in the du and er/sie/es forms: the **-b-** drops.
du ha**st**, er ha**t** (not habst/habt for er).
wir/sie/Sie use the full stem: **haben**.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you have the map? Yes, he has it.
cards.phrase: Hast du die Karte? Ja, er hat sie.

table.title: haben — Präsens
table.note: du hast / er hat — the -b- is dropped in these two forms.

cards.english: werden (to become / will) — full present-tense paradigm
cards.grammarNote:
**werden** has a vowel change in the du and er/sie/es forms: e → **i**.
du w**i**rst, er w**i**rd — note du form loses the -d- too.
wird is also the future auxiliary: Ich **werde** morgen lernen.
cards.englishPhrase: I become tired; you become hungry; he becomes a doctor.
cards.phrase: Ich werde müde; du wirst hungrig; er wird Arzt.

table.title: werden — Präsens
table.note: e → i in du/er forms; du wirst also loses the -d-.

cards.english: Stem-change e → ie: lesen (du liest, er liest)
cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs change their stem vowel in the **du** and **er/sie/es** forms only.
lesen: e → **ie** → du l**ie**st, er l**ie**st.
All other persons keep the original vowel: ich lese, wir lesen.
cards.englishPhrase: She reads the book; we read every day.
cards.phrase: Sie liest das Buch; wir lesen jeden Tag.

table.title: lesen — Präsens (e → ie)
table.note: Stem change e → ie in du and er/sie/es only.

cards.english: Stem-change e → i: sprechen and essen
cards.grammarNote:
Another vowel-change type: e → **i** in du and er/sie/es.
sprechen: du spr**i**chst, er spr**i**cht. essen: du **i**sst, er **i**sst.
Note essen: du isst has a double-s because the stem ends in -ss-.
cards.englishPhrase: He speaks German; she eats soup.
cards.phrase: Er spricht Deutsch; sie isst die Suppe.

table.title: sprechen · essen — Präsens (e → i)
table.note: e → i in du and er/sie/es for both verbs.

cards.english: Stem-change a → ä: fahren, schlafen, laufen
cards.grammarNote:
These verbs umlaut their stem vowel a → **ä** in du and er/sie/es.
fahren: du f**ä**hrst, er f**ä**hrt. schlafen: du schl**ä**fst. laufen: du l**ä**ufst.
wir/ihr/sie always keep the original a.
cards.englishPhrase: You drive the car; he sleeps well; she runs in the park.
cards.phrase: Du fährst das Auto; er schläft gut; sie läuft im Park.

table.title: fahren · schlafen · laufen — du / er form (a → ä)
table.note: a → ä only in du and er/sie/es. All other persons stay with a.

cards.english: Stem-changers: only du and er/sie/es change — wir/ihr/sie stay regular
cards.grammarNote:
The vowel change in stem-changing verbs is **limited to du and er/sie/es**.
wir, ihr, and sie/Sie always use the unchanged infinitive stem.
Contrast: du l**ie**st vs. wir les**en**; du f**ä**hrst vs. wir fahr**en**.
cards.englishPhrase: He reads, but we read together. She drives, but they drive too.
cards.phrase: Er liest, aber wir lesen zusammen. Sie fährt, aber sie fahren auch.

contrast.prompt: Stem-changers: du/er form vs. wir/sie form

a.term: du liest · er liest · du fährst · er fährt
a.gloss: stem changes in du and er/sie/es only

b.term: wir lesen · ihr lest · sie lesen · wir fahren · ihr fahrt · sie fahren
b.gloss: wir/ihr/sie always keep the original infinitive stem

cards.english: Present tense can also express a near future action
cards.grammarNote:
German present tense covers both **ongoing/habitual action** and **near-future plans**.
A time word like **morgen** (tomorrow) signals future meaning.
No future auxiliary is needed: Morgen spiele ich Fußball = I'm playing football tomorrow.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I'm playing football.
cards.phrase: Morgen spiele ich Fußball.

produce.concept: Present tense + time word = near future. No auxiliary needed.
produce.task: Say 'Tomorrow she is learning' and 'Tonight he is cooking' in German.
produce.answer: Morgen lernt sie. / Heute Abend kocht er.
produce.gloss: lernt = present of lernen (she), kocht = present of kochen (he)

cards.english: Choose the correct er/sie/es form of a stem-changing verb
cards.grammarNote:
schlafen belongs to the **a → ä** group.
Only the du and er/sie/es forms change: er schl**ä**ft.
Do not apply the umlaut to wir/ihr/sie forms.
cards.englishPhrase: The student sleeps in the library.
cards.phrase: Der Student ___ in der Bibliothek.

cloze.prompt: The student sleeps in the library. (schlafen, er/sie/es form)

cards.english: Produce: conjugate essen for ich, du, and er
cards.grammarNote:
essen has a stem change e → **i** in du and er/sie/es: du **isst**, er **isst**.
Note: ich esse is regular (no change in ich form).
du isst uses double-s because the stem is ess- and du adds -t.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat bread; you eat an apple; she eats soup.
cards.phrase: Ich esse Brot; du isst einen Apfel; sie isst die Suppe.

produce.concept: essen: e → i in du and er/sie/es. Stem ess- + du ending -t = isst.
produce.task: Give the present-tense forms of essen for ich, du, and er.
produce.answer: ich esse / du isst / er isst
produce.gloss: ich: regular -e ending; du + er: stem change e → i, ess- + t = isst

cards.english: Produce the du-form: one regular verb and one stem-changer
cards.grammarNote:
Regular du form: stem + **-st** (spiel- → spiel**st**).
Stem-changing du form: change vowel first, then + **-st** (les- → lies- → lies**t** — but les+st = liest, note no double-s here since stem ends in s, du adds only -t).
So: du spiel**st** (regular) vs. du l**ie**st (stem-changer, stem ends in s → only -t).
cards.englishPhrase: You play football and you read a book.
cards.phrase: Du spielst Fußball und du liest ein Buch.

produce.concept: Regular du: stem + -st. Stem-changer du: change vowel, then + -st (or just -t if stem ends in s/ß/z).
produce.task: Give the du-form of spielen (regular) and lesen (e → ie stem-changer).
produce.gloss: spielen: spiel + st = spielst. lesen: les → lies, stem ends in s → du liest (only -t added)

cards.english: The four German cases — what does each one do?
cards.grammarNote:
German has four cases that show a noun's role in the sentence.
**Nominativ** = the subject (who does the action)
**Akkusativ** = the direct object (thing directly affected)
**Dativ** = the indirect object (recipient / beneficiary)
**Genitiv** = possession ('of', 's)
cards.englishPhrase: Each case signals a different grammatical role.
cards.phrase: Jeder Fall zeigt eine andere grammatische Rolle.

table.title: The Four Cases
table.note: These four cases replace English word order signals.

cards.english: Definite article declension: der/die/das across all 4 cases and genders
cards.grammarNote:
The definite article changes form for each case and gender.
**Masc · Fem · Neut · Plural** — read across each row.
Dative plural adds **-n** to nouns that don't already end in -n.
cards.englishPhrase: The waiter brings the student the menu.
cards.phrase: Der Kellner bringt dem Studenten die Speisekarte.

table.title: Definite Articles — Masc / Fem / Neut / Plural
table.note: Masculine accusative (den) and all dative forms are the key changes to learn.

cards.english: Indefinite article ein-word declension across all 4 cases
cards.grammarNote:
**ein** follows the same pattern as **der/die/das** but drops the 'd-'.
Masculine Akkusativ: **einen** (not *ein*) — the most important form to memorize.
Genitiv adds **-es** (masc/neut) or **-er** (fem).
cards.englishPhrase: I need a teacher, a school, and a book.
cards.phrase: Ich brauche einen Lehrer, eine Schule und ein Buch.

table.title: Indefinite Articles — Masc / Fem / Neut
table.note: Plural uses keine (negation) or no article for 'some'.

cards.english: Nominative case — the subject of the sentence
cards.grammarNote:
The **Nominativ** marks the subject — whoever performs the action.
The verb always agrees with the Nominativ subject.
No article change from dictionary form: **der** Lehrer, **die** Milch, **das** Buch.
cards.englishPhrase: The teacher is reading a book.
cards.phrase: Der Lehrer liest ein Buch.

contrast.prompt: Which noun is the Nominativ subject?

cards.english: Accusative case — the direct object; masculine der → den is the key change
cards.grammarNote:
The **Akkusativ** marks the direct object — what is directly acted upon.
For feminine, neuter, and plural nouns the article looks identical to Nominativ.
Only **masculine** changes: **der → den** / **ein → einen**.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee is hot. — I drink the coffee.
cards.phrase: Der Kaffee ist heiß. — Ich trinke den Kaffee.

cards.english: Fill in the accusative article — masculine noun (der Apfel)
cards.grammarNote:
Masculine nouns take **den** (definite) or **einen** (indefinite) in the Akkusativ.
All other genders look the same as Nominativ.
Remember: the apple is masculine — **der** Apfel → **den** Apfel.
cards.englishPhrase: I am eating the apple.
cards.phrase: Ich esse ___ Apfel.

cloze.prompt: Accusative masculine definite article (der Apfel)

cards.english: Accusative feminine and neuter — article looks like nominative
cards.grammarNote:
Feminine and neuter definite articles **do not change** from Nominativ to Akkusativ.
**die** Milch stays **die** Milch; **das** Brot stays **das** Brot.
Only masculine changes — so spotting gender matters most for Akkusativ.
cards.englishPhrase: I am drinking the milk.
cards.phrase: Ich trinke ___ Milch.

cloze.prompt: Accusative feminine definite article (die Milch)

cards.english: Dative case — the indirect object / recipient
cards.grammarNote:
The **Dativ** marks the indirect object — who receives or benefits from the action.
Typical pattern: give/show/bring **someone** (Dat) **something** (Akk).
English uses 'to' or word order; German uses the Dativ form.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the waiter the bill.
cards.phrase: Ich gebe dem Kellner die Rechnung.

contrast.prompt: Who gets the action (Dativ) vs what is acted on (Akkusativ)?

cards.english: Dative article forms — dem / der / dem / den
cards.grammarNote:
In the **Dativ**: masc and neut take **dem**, fem takes **der**, plural takes **den**.
The indefinite articles mirror this: **einem / einer / einem**.
This is different from Nominativ/Akkusativ — all three look different here.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the student the menu.
cards.phrase: Ich gebe dem Studenten die Speisekarte.

table.title: Dative Articles — Masc / Fem / Neut / Plural
table.note: Plural dative: den + noun gains -n if it doesn't already end in -n or -s.

cards.english: Dative plural — den + noun adds -n (den Kindern style)
cards.grammarNote:
In the Dativ plural, the article is **den** AND the noun gains **-n** (if it doesn't already end in -n or -s).
This double-n signal is unique to dative plural.
Pool examples: **den Ärzten** (die Ärzte → den Ärzten), **den Büchern** (die Bücher → den Büchern).
cards.englishPhrase: I bring the doctors the medicine.
cards.phrase: Ich bringe den Ärzten das Medikament.

produce.task: Put 'die Bücher' and 'die Ärzte' into Dative plural
produce.gloss: die Bücher → den Büchern; die Ärzte → den Ärzten

cards.english: Contrast: accusative (direct object) vs dative (indirect object) with a give-verb
cards.grammarNote:
**geben** triggers both cases at once: Dat for the recipient, Akk for the thing.
Ask 'What is given?' → Akkusativ. Ask 'To whom?' → Dativ.
Same logic applies to **bringen**, **zeigen**, **schicken**.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the teacher the book.
cards.phrase: Ich gebe dem Lehrer das Buch.

a.term: Ich gebe dem Lehrer das Buch.
a.gloss: dem Lehrer = Dat (recipient); das Buch = Akk (thing)

b.term: Ich gebe das Buch dem Lehrer.
b.gloss: Same meaning — German allows both orders, case marks the role

cards.english: Fill in the dative article — helfen takes dative (not accusative!)
cards.grammarNote:
**helfen** (to help) always takes the **Dativ** — unlike English 'help someone' (Akk).
So: *Ich helfe dem Lehrer* — NOT *den Lehrer*.
Other Dativ-only verbs: **danken** (to thank), **gefallen** (to please).
cards.englishPhrase: I help the teacher.
cards.phrase: Ich helfe ___ Lehrer.

cloze.prompt: helfen takes Dative — masculine definite article

cards.english: Verbs that always take dative — helfen and danken
cards.grammarNote:
Some German verbs **always** take a Dativ object (no Akkusativ possible).
**helfen** — *Ich helfe dem Arzt.* (I help the doctor.)
**danken** — *Ich danke dem Kellner.* (I thank the waiter.)
cards.englishPhrase: I thank the doctor. / I help the waiter.
cards.phrase: Ich danke dem Arzt. Ich helfe dem Kellner.

produce.task: Say 'I help the teacher' and 'I thank the student' using dative articles
produce.answer: Ich helfe dem Lehrer. / Ich danke dem Studenten.
produce.gloss: helfen + dem Lehrer (Dat masc); danken + dem Studenten (Dat masc)

cards.english: Genitive case — possession; masc/neut noun adds -s or -es
cards.grammarNote:
The **Genitiv** expresses possession or belonging — like 's or 'of' in English.
Masculine and neuter nouns add **-s** (or **-es** after sibilants/short syllables).
*das Auto des Lehrers* = the teacher's car. Articles: **des / der / des / der**.
cards.englishPhrase: The teacher's car is in the parking lot.
cards.phrase: Das Auto des Lehrers ist auf dem Parkplatz.

cards.english: Personal pronouns across Nominativ, Akkusativ, and Dativ
cards.word: ich / mich / mir · du / dich / dir · er / ihn / ihm
cards.grammarNote:
Pronouns change form for each case, just like articles.
**Nom → Akk → Dat**: ich→mich→mir, du→dich→dir, er→ihn→ihm.
Memorize *ihn* (him, Akk) vs *ihm* (him, Dat) — a very common mix-up.
cards.englishPhrase: He sees me. / I give him the book.
cards.phrase: Er sieht mich. Ich gebe ihm das Buch.
literal: He sees me — mich = Akk of ich
I give him the book — ihm = Dat of er

table.title: Personal Pronouns — Nom / Akk / Dat
table.note: Format: Akkusativ / Dativ. Nominativ is the dictionary form in the label.

cards.english: Produce: put 'der Apfel' into accusative and dative (definite article)
cards.grammarNote:
**der Apfel** is masculine (der-word).
Akkusativ: **den** Apfel — the direct object (you eat it).
Dativ: **dem** Apfel — the indirect object (you give something to it, or after certain verbs/prepositions).
cards.englishPhrase: I eat the apple. / I give something to the apple.
cards.phrase: Ich esse den Apfel. / Ich gebe dem Apfel ...

produce.task: Give the Akkusativ and Dativ forms of 'der Apfel'
produce.gloss: der → den in Akkusativ; der → dem in Dativ

cards.english: Perfekt structure: auxiliary at position 2, Partizip II at the end
cards.grammarNote:
The **Perfekt** is German's main spoken past tense.
Formula: **haben/sein** (position 2) + … + **Partizip II** (very end).
The auxiliary carries the tense; the Partizip II never moves from the final slot.
cards.englishPhrase: I drank coffee. (lit. I have coffee drunk.)
cards.phrase: Ich habe Kaffee getrunken.

contrast.prompt: Where do the two verbs sit?

cards.english: Regular Partizip II: ge- + stem + -t
cards.grammarNote:
Most verbs form the Partizip II with **ge-** prefix and **-t** ending.
Stem = infinitive minus **-en**.
Example: kochen → **ge**koch**t**, spielen → **ge**spiel**t**, lernen → **ge**lern**t**.
cards.englishPhrase: She cooked soup and played music.
cards.phrase: Sie hat Suppe gekocht und Musik gespielt.

table.title: Regular Partizip II (ge- + stem + -t)
table.note: Drop -en, add ge- before and -t after the stem.

cards.english: Build the regular Partizip II of 'arbeiten'
cards.grammarNote:
When the stem ends in **-t** or **-d**, insert an extra **-e-** before the **-t** ending to keep the word pronounceable.
arbeiten → stem **arbeit** → **ge**arbeit**et**.
cards.englishPhrase: He worked in the office today.
cards.phrase: Er hat heute im Büro ___.

cloze.prompt: Regular Partizip II of arbeiten (stem ends in -t, so add -et)

cards.english: Strong Partizip II: ge- + (often changed) stem + -en
cards.grammarNote:
Strong verbs use **-en** as the Partizip II ending, and many show a **vowel change** in the stem.
These must be memorised individually — the ge- prefix still appears.
Examples: trinken → **getrunken**, essen → **gegessen**, lesen → **gelesen**.
cards.englishPhrase: I drank water, ate fish, and read the menu.
cards.phrase: Ich habe Wasser getrunken, Fisch gegessen und die Speisekarte gelesen.

table.title: Strong Partizip II (ge- + stem + -en)
table.note: Vowel change: trinken i→u, essen e→e(ss), singen i→u, schwimmen i→o. Lesen keeps e.

cards.english: Give the Partizip II of 'essen' and 'lesen'
cards.grammarNote:
Both are strong verbs ending in **-en**.
**essen** (stem ess): vowel e stays but ss kept → **gegessen**.
**lesen** (stem les): vowel e unchanged → **gelesen**.
cards.englishPhrase: We ate bread and read the book.
cards.phrase: Wir haben Brot gegessen und das Buch gelesen.

produce.concept: Strong Partizip II: ge- + changed stem + -en
produce.task: Give the Partizip II of 'essen' and 'lesen'
produce.gloss: essen → gegessen, lesen → gelesen

cards.english: haben as the default Perfekt auxiliary — full present tense
cards.grammarNote:
**haben** is the auxiliary for most verbs (transitive, and many intransitive).
Conjugate **haben** in the present; the Partizip II sits at the end.
Example: **Ich habe** Kaffee getrunken.
cards.englishPhrase: I have drunk coffee. / Du hast … / Er hat …
cards.phrase: Ich habe Kaffee getrunken.

table.title: haben — present (Perfekt auxiliary)
table.note: Perfekt: habe/hast/hat/... + Partizip II at end.

cards.english: sein as auxiliary: motion and change-of-state verbs
cards.grammarNote:
Verbs of **motion from A to B** (gehen, laufen, fahren, reisen, kommen, schwimmen) and **change of state** take **sein**, not haben.
Conjugate **sein** normally; Partizip II still goes to the end.
Tip: if you can ask 'where to?', think sein.
cards.englishPhrase: She went to school. He ran to the park.
cards.phrase: Sie ist zur Schule gegangen. Er ist in den Park gelaufen.

table.title: sein — Perfekt auxiliaries (motion/change verbs)
table.note: *schwimmen can also take haben when no destination is stated.

cards.english: Contrast: haben vs sein as Perfekt auxiliary
cards.grammarNote:
**haben** = most verbs (eating, drinking, working, playing).
**sein** = motion/travel verbs and change-of-state.
Both place the Partizip II at the very end of the clause.
cards.englishPhrase: I ate. vs I ran.
cards.phrase: Ich habe gegessen. vs Ich bin gelaufen.

a.gloss: haben — essen is transitive, no motion

b.gloss: sein — laufen is motion from A to B

cards.english: Choose haben or sein: travel to Berlin
cards.grammarNote:
**fahren** (to travel/drive) signals directed motion → auxiliary is **sein**.
Remember: the form must agree with the subject.
*ich* → **bin**.
cards.englishPhrase: I travelled to Berlin.
cards.phrase: Ich ___ nach Berlin gefahren.

cloze.prompt: fahren = directed motion → which auxiliary for 'ich'?

cards.english: Verbs ending in -ieren: NO ge- prefix
cards.grammarNote:
Verbs ending in **-ieren** already have a stressed non-native suffix, so they drop the **ge-** prefix.
Ending is still **-t** (weak).
studieren → **studiert**, fotografieren → **fotografiert**.
cards.englishPhrase: She studied at the university and photographed the museum.
cards.phrase: Sie hat an der Universität studiert und das Museum fotografiert.

table.title: -ieren verbs: NO ge- prefix
table.note: Rule: -ieren verbs skip ge- but keep the -t ending.

cards.english: Inseparable-prefix verbs (be-, ver-, …): NO ge- prefix
cards.grammarNote:
Verbs with inseparable prefixes (**be-, ver-, ent-, er-, ge-, zer-**) never add **ge-**.
The prefix itself is stressed enough to block ge-.
bestellen → **bestellt**, verdienen → **verdient**, verstehen → **verstanden**.
cards.englishPhrase: He ordered soup, earned money, and understood the menu.
cards.phrase: Er hat Suppe bestellt, Geld verdient und die Speisekarte verstanden.

table.title: Inseparable-prefix verbs: NO ge-
table.note: Prefixes be-, ver-, ... block the ge- prefix entirely.

cards.english: Form the Partizip II of 'bestellen' (inseparable prefix)
cards.grammarNote:
**bestellen** has the inseparable prefix **be-**, so no ge- is added.
Weak verb: stem **bestell** + **-t** → **bestellt**.
Never *gebestellt*.
cards.englishPhrase: They ordered coffee and tea.
cards.phrase: Sie haben Kaffee und Tee ___.

cloze.prompt: Partizip II of bestellen — inseparable prefix, no ge-

cards.english: Word order: Partizip II always goes to the very end
cards.grammarNote:
No matter how many adverbs or objects appear, the **Partizip II is always last**.
If the sentence starts with a time adverb (V2 rule), **haben/sein** moves to position 2 and Partizip II still ends the clause.
**Gestern** habe ich Fußball **gespielt**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I played football.
cards.phrase: Gestern habe ich Fußball gespielt.

produce.concept: Partizip II stays at the very end; auxiliary at position 2
produce.task: Rearrange into a correct Perfekt sentence: gestern / ich / Fußball / spielen
produce.gloss: Adverb first → habe shifts to pos. 2 → Partizip II last

cards.english: Contrast: regular (gemacht-type) vs strong (getrunken-type) Partizip II
cards.grammarNote:
**Regular**: ge- + stem + **-t** — stem is unchanged.
**Strong**: ge- + **changed stem** + **-en** — vowel often shifts.
When in doubt about a strong verb, check the dictionary.
cards.englishPhrase: She made lunch and drank coffee.
cards.phrase: Sie hat das Mittagessen gemacht und Kaffee getrunken.

cards.english: Put 'Ich spiele Fußball' into the Perfekt
cards.grammarNote:
**spielen** is regular: Partizip II = **gespielt** (ge + spiel + t).
Auxiliary = **haben** (no motion, no change of state).
Result: **Ich habe** Fußball **gespielt**.
cards.englishPhrase: I played football.
cards.phrase: Ich habe Fußball gespielt.

produce.concept: Regular verb + haben auxiliary → Perfekt
produce.task: Convert to Perfekt: Ich spiele Fußball.
produce.gloss: spielen → gespielt (regular); auxiliary haben; Partizip II at end

cards.english: Put 'Ich gehe ins Kino' into the Perfekt
cards.grammarNote:
**gehen** is a motion verb → auxiliary **sein**.
PartizipII of gehen is **gegangen** (strong, irregular: ge + gang + en).
Result: **Ich bin** ins Kino **gegangen**.
cards.englishPhrase: I went to the cinema.
cards.phrase: Ich bin ins Kino gegangen.

produce.concept: Motion verb + sein auxiliary → Perfekt
produce.task: Convert to Perfekt: Ich gehe ins Kino.
produce.gloss: gehen = motion → sein; gegangen (strong, ge+gang+en)

cards.english: How do modal verbs work in German?
cards.grammarNote:
The **modal verb** goes in position 2 (conjugated). The main verb goes to the **end** as an infinitive.
Pattern: Subject + **Modal** + … + Infinitive
Negation: add **nicht** before the infinitive.
cards.englishPhrase: I can speak German.
cards.phrase: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.

produce.concept: Modal (position 2, conjugated) + main verb INFINITIVE at the end
produce.task: Where do the modal verb and main verb go in: 'She wants to learn German'?
produce.gloss: Modal 'will' in position 2; infinitive 'lernen' at the end

cards.english: können — present tense conjugation (can / be able to)
cards.grammarNote:
**können** = can / be able to. Note: **ich** and **er/sie/es** share the same form and have NO personal ending.
Vowel changes: ö → a in the singular (ich **kann**, du **kannst**, er **kann**).
cards.englishPhrase: Can you swim?
cards.phrase: Kannst du schwimmen?

table.title: können — present
table.note: ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no personal ending.

cards.english: müssen — present tense conjugation (must / have to)
cards.grammarNote:
**müssen** = must / have to. Again **ich** and **er/sie/es** share the same endingless form.
Vowel: ü → u in the singular (ich **muss**, du **musst**, er **muss**).
cards.englishPhrase: She has to work today.
cards.phrase: Sie muss heute arbeiten.

table.title: müssen — present
table.note: ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no personal ending.

cards.english: wollen — present tense conjugation (want to)
cards.grammarNote:
**wollen** = to want (to do something). Vowel: o → i in singular (ich **will**, du **willst**, er **will**).
**ich** and **er/sie/es** are identical with no ending — same pattern as all modals.
cards.englishPhrase: He wants to travel.
cards.phrase: Er will reisen.

table.title: wollen — present
table.note: ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no personal ending.

cards.english: dürfen — present tense conjugation (may / be allowed to)
cards.grammarNote:
**dürfen** = may / be allowed to (permission). Vowel: ü → a in singular (ich **darf**, du **darfst**, er **darf**).
Always identical endingless forms for **ich** and **er/sie/es**.
cards.englishPhrase: Are we allowed to eat here?
cards.phrase: Dürfen wir hier essen?

table.title: dürfen — present
table.note: ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no personal ending.

cards.english: sollen — present tense conjugation (should / supposed to)
cards.grammarNote:
**sollen** = should / be supposed to (often from an external expectation or instruction).
Unusually, **no vowel change** in the singular: ich **soll**, du **sollst**, er **soll**.
**ich** and **er/sie/es** still have no personal ending.
cards.englishPhrase: You are supposed to learn the words.
cards.phrase: Du sollst die Wörter lernen.

table.title: sollen — present
table.note: No vowel change in sollen — the only modal with an unchanged stem.

cards.english: mögen — present tense conjugation (to like)
cards.grammarNote:
**mögen** = to like (something/someone). Used with a noun object, not an infinitive.
Vowel: ö → a in singular (ich **mag**, du **magst**, er **mag**).
Do NOT add a second verb after mögen — use **möchten** for 'would like to do'.
cards.englishPhrase: I like the music.
cards.phrase: Ich mag die Musik.

table.title: mögen — present
table.note: mögen typically takes a noun object. For 'would like to do', use möchten.

cards.english: möchten — present tense conjugation (would like — polite)
cards.grammarNote:
**möchten** = would like to (polite). It is the Konjunktiv II of mögen but used as a standalone polite modal.
Forms: ich **möchte**, du **möchtest**, er **möchte** — note **er/sie/es** ends in **-e**, unlike other modals.
Use it with an infinitive at the end: Ich möchte Kaffee **bestellen**.
cards.englishPhrase: I would like to order coffee.
cards.phrase: Ich möchte Kaffee bestellen.

table.title: möchten — present
table.note: er/sie/es ends in -e (möchte), unlike other modals which have no ending.

cards.english: The shared pattern: ich = er/sie/es, no personal ending, vowel change
cards.grammarNote:
All modals: **ich** and **er/sie/es** share the same form and have **no personal ending**.
Singular vowel change (umlaut dropped): können→**kann**, müssen→**muss**, wollen→**will**, dürfen→**darf**, mögen→**mag**.
Exception: **sollen** has no vowel change; **möchten** keeps the umlaut and adds -e for er.
cards.englishPhrase: I can / he can — I must / he must.
cards.phrase: Ich kann / er kann — ich muss / er muss.

cards.english: Modal sentence: fill in the missing infinitive at the end
cards.grammarNote:
The main verb always goes to the **end** as an infinitive when a modal is present.
The modal is conjugated and takes position 2.
cards.englishPhrase: I have to work today.
cards.phrase: Ich muss heute ___.

cloze.prompt: I have to work today. (put the correct infinitive at the end)

cards.english: können (ability) vs dürfen (permission) — what's the difference?
cards.grammarNote:
**können** = physical/mental ability — 'I am able to'.
**dürfen** = permission — 'I am allowed to'.
Example trap: 'Ich kann hier essen' (I am physically able to eat here) vs 'Ich darf hier essen' (I am allowed to eat here).
cards.englishPhrase: I can swim. / I'm allowed to swim here.
cards.phrase: Ich kann schwimmen. / Ich darf hier schwimmen.

a.gloss: können = ability (I am able to swim)

b.gloss: dürfen = permission (I am allowed to swim here)

cards.english: müssen (must — inner/logical necessity) vs sollen (should — external expectation)
cards.grammarNote:
**müssen** = strong internal or logical necessity — 'I have to / must'.
**sollen** = external obligation or instruction — 'I'm supposed to / should'.
If your doctor says 'eat vegetables', that is **sollen** (you were told to), not müssen.
cards.englishPhrase: I have to sleep. / I'm supposed to sleep (the doctor said so).
cards.phrase: Ich muss schlafen. / Ich soll schlafen.

b.gloss: sollen = I'm supposed to (told by someone else)

cards.english: Build a German modal sentence: ich + können + schwimmen
cards.grammarNote: Steps: 1) conjugate the modal for the subject (**ich** → **kann**). 2) Place it in position 2. 3) Send the main verb to the **end** as an infinitive.
cards.englishPhrase: I can swim.
cards.phrase: Ich kann schwimmen.

produce.concept: Subject + conjugated modal (pos. 2) + ... + infinitive (end)
produce.task: Build a sentence from: ich + können + schwimmen
produce.gloss: können → kann for ich; schwimmen stays as infinitive at the end

cards.english: Word order with a time phrase: 'Today I want to play football'
cards.grammarNote:
When a time phrase (heute, jetzt, morgen…) starts the sentence, it takes **position 1**.
The **modal verb still stays in position 2** (verb-second rule). The infinitive stays at the **end**.
Structure: Heute + **will** + ich + Fußball + **spielen**.
cards.englishPhrase: Today I want to play football.
cards.phrase: Heute will ich Fußball spielen.

cloze.prompt: Today I want to play football. (verb-second rule — pick the correct word order)

cards.english: mögen (I like X — noun) vs möchten (I would like to — + infinitive)
cards.grammarNote:
**mögen** takes a **noun** object: Ich mag den Fisch. (I like the fish.)
**möchten** takes an **infinitive** at the end: Ich möchte Fisch essen. (I would like to eat fish.)
Do not say *Ich mag essen — that is unnatural in modern German for this meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: I like the fish. / I would like to eat fish.
cards.phrase: Ich mag den Fisch. / Ich möchte Fisch essen.

contrast.prompt: Like a noun vs would like to do something

a.gloss: mögen + noun object (I like the fish)

b.gloss: möchten + infinitive at end (I would like to eat fish)

cards.english: The V2 rule: the conjugated verb is always the second element in a German main clause
cards.grammarNote:
In every German main clause, the **conjugated verb** occupies exactly the **second position** (not necessarily the second word).
The first position can be the subject, a time phrase, an adverb — anything — but the verb always comes second.
This is the most fundamental rule of German sentence structure.
cards.englishPhrase: I drink coffee in the morning.
cards.phrase: Ich trinke Kaffee am Morgen.

table.title: V2 — position 2 is always the verb
table.note: Whatever sits in position 1, the verb stays at position 2.

cards.english: Subject-first order: Subject + Verb + rest of sentence
cards.grammarNote:
The default word order is **Subject → Verb → Object/rest**.
This is called SVO order and feels most natural to English speakers.
The subject is in position 1, the verb is in position 2.
cards.englishPhrase: She reads a book in the library.
cards.phrase: Sie liest ein Buch in der Bibliothek.

produce.concept: Subject (pos.1) + conjugated verb (pos.2) + rest
produce.task: Put these words in default SVO order: 'Kaffee / trinkt / er / am Morgen'
produce.gloss: Er (subject, pos.1) → trinkt (verb, pos.2) → Kaffee am Morgen (rest)

cards.english: Inversion: when a time or place phrase leads, the subject moves after the verb
cards.grammarNote:
If you move a time or place phrase to **position 1**, the subject must jump to **position 3** — right after the verb.
The verb stays locked at position 2 no matter what comes first.
This flip is called **inversion** and is very common in German.
cards.englishPhrase: In the morning I drink coffee.
cards.phrase: Am Morgen trinke ich Kaffee.

contrast.prompt: Normal order vs. fronted time phrase

b.gloss: time phrase first → verb stays pos.2, subject moves to pos.3

cards.english: Cloze: 'Heute' opens the sentence — place the verb in position 2
cards.grammarNote:
**Heute** (today) fills position 1, so the conjugated verb must immediately follow at position 2.
The subject 'ich' is pushed to position 3.
cards.englishPhrase: Today I play football.
cards.phrase: Heute spiele ich Fußball.

cloze.prompt: Heute opens the clause — what verb form fills the blank?

cards.english: Yes/No questions: the conjugated verb moves to position 1
cards.grammarNote:
To form a yes/no question, move the verb to **position 1** — before the subject.
There is no 'do/does' helper verb like in English; the conjugated verb simply leads.
The subject follows immediately in position 2.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you drink coffee?
cards.phrase: Trinkst du Kaffee?

cards.english: W-questions: question word + verb + subject (+ rest)
cards.grammarNote:
W-questions follow the **V2 rule**: the question word is position 1, the verb is position 2, the subject comes third.
Common W-words: **wer, was, wo, wann, warum, wie**.
Example: Wo → arbeitest → du?

cards.english: TMP order in the middle field: Time → Manner → Place
cards.grammarNote:
When multiple adverbials appear in the middle field, German prefers **Time → Manner → Place**.
Think: *When? → How? → Where?*
"Ich fahre **heute** (time) **mit dem Bus** (manner) **zur Arbeit** (place)."

cards.english: Separable verbs: the prefix is split off and goes to the very end of the clause
cards.grammarNote:
Many German verbs have a separable prefix: **auf-**, **ein-**, **an-**, **auf-**, etc.
In a main clause, the conjugated stem goes to **position 2** and the prefix jumps to **the end**.
Example: *aufstehen* → "Ich **stehe** um sieben **auf**."
cards.englishPhrase: I get up at seven.
cards.phrase: Ich stehe um sieben auf.

table.title: Separable verbs — prefix to the end
table.note: Conjugated stem at pos. 2; prefix stranded at the end.

cards.english: Contrast: separable verb in infinitive form vs. split in conjugated main clause
cards.grammarNote:
In the **infinitive**, the prefix is attached: *auf·stehen*.
In a **conjugated main clause**, the prefix detaches and moves to the end: *Ich **stehe** um sieben **auf**.*
The gap between stem and prefix can be wide — the prefix always waits at the very end.
cards.englishPhrase: I need to get up early vs. I get up at seven.
cards.phrase: aufstehen vs. Ich stehe um sieben auf.

b.gloss: conjugated — stem at pos.2, prefix at end

cards.english: Modal verbs: modal at position 2, dependent infinitive at the end (Satzklammer)
cards.grammarNote:
When a modal verb (können, möchten, …) is used, the **modal** is conjugated and sits at **position 2**.
The full infinitive of the main verb is pushed to the **very end** of the clause — forming a bracket (*Satzklammer*).
Example: "Ich **kann** gut **schwimmen**."
cards.englishPhrase: I can swim well.
cards.phrase: Ich kann gut schwimmen.

cards.english: Perfekt: auxiliary 'haben/sein' at position 2, Partizip II at the end
cards.grammarNote:
The **Perfekt** tense uses a bracket just like modals: the auxiliary (**haben** or **sein**) is conjugated at **position 2** and the **Partizip II** goes to the **end**.
Example: "Ich **habe** Fußball **gespielt**."
This bracket structure applies to all compound tenses in German.
cards.englishPhrase: I played football.
cards.phrase: Ich habe Fußball gespielt.

produce.concept: haben/sein (pos.2) + ... + Partizip II (end)

cards.english: Subordinate clauses with 'weil/dass': conjugated verb goes to the very end
cards.grammarNote:
Conjunctions like **weil** (because) and **dass** (that) introduce subordinate clauses.
In a subordinate clause, the **conjugated verb is kicked to the very end** — position 1 is the conjunction.
Example: "Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**."
cards.englishPhrase: I stay at home because I am sick.
cards.phrase: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.

b.gloss: subordinate clause — verb moved to the end

cards.english: Cloze: complete the weil-clause by placing the verb at the end
cards.grammarNote:
In a **weil**-clause, the conjugated verb occupies the **final position**.
The word order inside the clause is: conjunction → subject → rest → **verb**.
cards.englishPhrase: I sleep because I am tired.
cards.phrase: Ich schlafe, weil ich müde bin.

cloze.prompt: Verb goes to the end in a weil-clause

cards.english: Coordinating conjunctions und/aber/oder do NOT change word order
cards.grammarNote:
**Und** (and), **aber** (but), and **oder** (or) are coordinating conjunctions — they occupy **position 0** and do not affect the word order of the clause that follows.
The next clause keeps normal V2 order: subject then verb.
Contrast this with **weil/dass**, which send the verb to the end.
cards.englishPhrase: I am tired but I work.
cards.phrase: Ich bin müde, aber ich arbeite.

a.gloss: coordinating — normal V2 order preserved after aber

b.gloss: subordinating — verb sent to the end

cards.english: Predicate vs. attributive adjectives: when do endings appear?
cards.grammarNote:
After **sein** (and other linking verbs), the adjective is *predicate* — it takes **no ending**: *Der Kaffee ist heiß.*
Before a noun, the adjective is *attributive* — it **must take an ending**: *der heiße Kaffee.*
The ending depends on the article type and the noun's gender/case.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee is hot. / the hot coffee
cards.phrase: Der Kaffee ist heiß. / der heiße Kaffee

cards.english: Weak adjective endings — after a definite article (der/die/das)
cards.grammarNote:
After a definite article, the article already signals gender/case, so the adjective takes a **light** ending.
Rule: **-e** in nominative singular (all genders) and accusative feminine/neuter; **-en** everywhere else.
Think of it as: the article does the work, the adjective just adds -e or -en.
cards.englishPhrase: the hot coffee / the cold milk / the cold water
cards.phrase: der heiße Kaffee / die kalte Milch / das kalte Wasser

table.title: Weak endings (after der/die/das)
table.note: Only -e or -en. The definite article carries the full case signal.

cards.english: Weak endings — nominative singular examples for all three genders
cards.grammarNote:
In the **nominative singular**, weak adjectives always end in **-e** — regardless of gender.
The definite article (der / die / das) already marks the gender, so -e is enough.
Compare: *der heiße* Kaffee, *die kalte* Milch, *das kalte* Wasser.
cards.englishPhrase: the hot coffee / the cold milk / the cold water
cards.phrase: der heiße Kaffee / die kalte Milch / das kalte Wasser

table.title: Weak: nominative singular
table.note: All three take -e in nominative after a definite article.

cards.english: Weak ending: accusative masculine after definite article → fill the blank
cards.grammarNote:
Accusative masculine is one of the **-en** cases in the weak pattern.
The definite article changes: *der* → *den* (masc acc), and the adjective also takes **-en**.
Both the article and adjective end in -en: *Ich trinke den heißen Kaffee.*

cards.phrase: Ich trinke den heißen Kaffee.

cards.english: Mixed adjective endings — after ein-words (ein/kein/mein…)
cards.grammarNote:
Ein-words have **no ending** in 3 spots (masc nom, neut nom, neut acc) — so the adjective must show gender there.
In all other positions, ein-words do show gender → adjective takes weak -e/-en.
Mixed = mostly weak, but **-er / -es** where ein is bare.
cards.englishPhrase: a hot coffee / a sour soup / cold water
cards.phrase: ein heißer Kaffee / eine saure Suppe / ein kaltes Wasser

table.title: Mixed endings (after ein/kein/mein)
table.note: Three spots differ from weak: masc nom -er, neut nom -es, neut acc -es.

cards.english: Mixed ending: neuter nominative after 'ein' → fill the blank
cards.grammarNote:
**ein** has no ending in neuter nominative — it gives no gender signal.
The adjective must compensate with **-es** (mirroring *das* → -s signal).
*Ein kaltes Wasser, bitte.* — The -es ending is what tells us it's neuter.
cards.englishPhrase: A cold water, please.
cards.phrase: Ein kaltes Wasser, bitte.

cloze.prompt: A cold water, please (neut nominative — mixed ending)

cards.english: Weak vs. mixed: masculine nominative — spot the difference
cards.grammarNote:
After **der** (weak): *der heiße Kaffee* — the article *der* already signals masculine, so adjective takes light **-e**.
After **ein** (mixed): *ein heißer Kaffee* — *ein* has no ending here, so adjective takes **-er** to show masculine.
Pattern: if the article shows gender, use -e; if it doesn't, the adjective must step up.
cards.englishPhrase: the hot coffee / a hot coffee
cards.phrase: der heiße Kaffee / ein heißer Kaffee

a.gloss: weak: der signals masc → adj takes -e

b.gloss: mixed: ein is bare → adj takes -er

cards.english: Strong adjective endings — no article at all
cards.grammarNote:
When there is **no article**, the adjective alone must carry the full case/gender signal.
Strong endings mirror the definite article endings (der→-er, die→-e, das→-es, dem→-em, etc.).
Common in recipes, headlines, menus: *Heißer Kaffee*, *Kalte Milch*, *Gute Suppe*.
cards.englishPhrase: hot coffee / cold milk / cold water / good soup
cards.phrase: heißer Kaffee / kalte Milch / kaltes Wasser / gute Suppe

table.title: Strong endings: nominative singular (no article)
table.note: Strong endings copy the definite article signal. No article means adjective does all the work.

cards.english: Strong endings in accusative and dative (no article)
cards.grammarNote:
Strong adjectives follow the full definite-article pattern in every case.
**Accusative**: masc -en (heißen Kaffee), fem -e (kalte Milch), neut -es (kaltes Wasser).
**Dative**: all genders take **-em** (masc/neut) or **-er** (fem): *mit heißem Kaffee, mit kalter Milch*.
cards.englishPhrase: I drink hot coffee. / with cold milk
cards.phrase: Ich trinke heißen Kaffee. / mit kalter Milch
literal: with cold milk (-er fem dat strong)

table.title: Strong endings: accusative and dative (no article)
table.note: Strong endings mirror the definite article. Acc masc -en, fem -e, neut -es. Dat masc/neut -em, fem -er.

cards.english: Strong vs. weak: masculine nominative — no article vs. definite article
cards.grammarNote:
**Strong** (no article): *guter Wein* — adjective takes -er to signal masculine nominative.
**Weak** (after der): *der gute Wein* — article *der* already signals masculine, adjective takes -e.
The total case information must always be expressed — either by article, adjective, or both.
cards.englishPhrase: good wine (no article) / the good wine
cards.phrase: guter Wein / der gute Wein
literal: weak: article carries it, adj takes -e

b.gloss: weak: der signals masc → adjective takes -e

cards.english: Adjective endings in the plural
cards.grammarNote:
**After a definite/ein-word article** (die Tomaten, keine Äpfel): adjective always takes **-en**.
**No article** (strong plural): adjective takes **-e** in nominative/accusative, **-en** in dative.
In practice, plurals with an article are very common — remember: article present → -en.
cards.englishPhrase: the sour tomatoes / sour tomatoes (no article)
cards.phrase: die sauren Tomaten / saure Tomaten

table.title: Plural adjective endings
table.note: Article present → always -en in plural. No article nom/acc pl → -e.

cards.english: Plural ending after definite article → fill the blank
cards.grammarNote:
After a definite article in the plural, the adjective **always** ends in **-en**.
*die leckeren Tomaten* — the article *die* is there, so the adjective takes -en.
This rule holds for all cases in the plural when an article is present.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat the delicious tomatoes.
cards.phrase: Ich esse die leckeren Tomaten.

cloze.prompt: I eat the delicious tomatoes (plural after definite article)

cards.english: Summary rule: how to choose -e vs -en vs strong ending
cards.grammarNote:
**Key rule of thumb**: Is the case/gender already shown by the article?
→ Yes (strong article ending): adjective takes **-e** (nom/acc) or **-en** (elsewhere).
→ No (article bare or absent): adjective takes a **strong ending** that mirrors *der/die/das/dem/den*.
cards.englishPhrase: The article does the work; the adjective just follows.
cards.phrase: der heiße Kaffee / ein heißer Kaffee / heißer Kaffee

table.title: Choosing the adjective ending
table.note: If the article already carries the gender flag, the adjective can stay light (-e/-en).

cards.english: Produce: decline 'kalt' before 'das Wasser' — weak (def. article) vs. strong (no article)
cards.grammarNote:
**Weak** (after *das*): *das kalte Wasser* — *das* shows neuter, so adjective takes **-e**.
**Strong** (no article): *kaltes Wasser* — adjective must show neuter itself → **-es** mirrors *das*.
Both are nominative neuter; only the presence/absence of the article changes the ending.
cards.englishPhrase: the cold water (weak) / cold water (strong)
cards.phrase: das kalte Wasser / kaltes Wasser

cards.english: Produce: give the mixed ending for 'süß' before 'der Apfel' after 'ein' (masc nom)
cards.grammarNote:
**ein** + masculine nominative: *ein* has no ending here → the adjective must show masculine.
The strong masculine nominative ending mirrors *der* → **-er**.
So: *ein süßer Apfel* — the adjective alone signals that this is masculine nominative.

cards.english: The core negation rule: kein vs. nicht
cards.grammarNote:
Use **kein** to negate a noun that would take **ein** or no article: 'Ich habe Hunger' → 'Ich habe **keinen** Hunger'.
Use **nicht** to negate everything else: verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and nouns with a definite article.
**kein** declines like **ein**; **nicht** is invariable.
cards.englishPhrase: I have no money. / I don't drink coffee.
cards.phrase: Ich habe kein Geld. / Ich trinke nicht.

a.gloss: kein = negates noun with no article

cards.english: kein declension — it declines exactly like ein
cards.grammarNote:
**kein** takes the same endings as **ein** across all cases and genders.
Nominative: kein / keine / kein / keine (m/f/n/pl).
Accusative masculine changes: **keinen**; feminine and neuter stay keine / kein.
cards.englishPhrase: No doctor / No music / No book / No friends
cards.phrase: kein Arzt / keine Musik / kein Buch / keine Freunde

table.note: Dative: keinem (m/n), keiner (f), keinen+n (pl). Pattern mirrors ein.

cards.grammarNote:
**das Geld** is neuter. In accusative position after **haben**, neuter stays **kein** (same as nominative).

cards.english: kein negates the noun (no article) — nicht negates a definite noun
cards.grammarNote:
When the noun has **no article**, use **kein**: 'Ich trinke **keinen** Kaffee.'
When the noun has a **definite article** (den/die/das), use **nicht** after it: 'Ich trinke den Kaffee **nicht**.'
Both mean 'I don't drink the/any coffee' but signal different things.

cards.phrase: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee. / Ich trinke den Kaffee nicht.

a.gloss: kein negates noun with no article (masc acc → keinen)

cards.english: nicht negating the whole sentence — goes near the END
cards.grammarNote:
To negate an entire sentence or verb, **nicht** moves to the **end** of the sentence (or just before the final verb part).
'Ich arbeite heute **nicht**.' = I am not working today.
Time adverbs like **heute** come before nicht.
cards.englishPhrase: I am not working today.
cards.phrase: Ich arbeite heute nicht.

cards.english: nicht before the specific element it negates (adjective / adverb)
cards.grammarNote:
When **nicht** targets a specific adjective or adverb, it stands **directly before** that element.
'Das ist **nicht** gut.' = That is not good.
Contrast: 'Ich arbeite nicht' (whole verb) vs. 'Das ist nicht gut' (the adjective gut).

cards.phrase: Das ist nicht gut. / Die Suppe ist nicht heiß.

b.gloss: nicht at the end — negates the whole verb

cards.english: nicht with modal + infinitive — nicht before the infinitive
cards.grammarNote:
With a modal verb (können, möchten…) + infinitive, **nicht** comes **before the infinitive** at the end.
'Ich kann **nicht** schwimmen.' = I cannot swim.
The infinitive stays at the very end; nicht slots in just before it.

cards.phrase: Ich kann nicht schwimmen.

cards.english: Place nicht correctly: 'I am not reading the book.'

**kein** = nicht + ein, fully merged.

cards.english: The 9 two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen) and their meanings
cards.grammarNote:
These 9 prepositions can take **Akkusativ** OR **Dativ** depending on meaning.
The key question: **wohin?** (where to?) → Akkusativ; **wo?** (where?) → Dativ.
They describe position/movement in space.
cards.englishPhrase: Two-way prepositions: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen
cards.phrase: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen

table.title: The 9 Wechselpräpositionen
table.note: All 9 can be either accusative or dative depending on motion vs. location.

cards.english: THE RULE: when do two-way prepositions take Akkusativ vs. Dativ?
cards.grammarNote:
**Wohin?** (where to? / motion toward a place) → **Akkusativ**.
**Wo?** (where? / static location) → **Dativ**.
Ask the question first, then choose the case.

cards.grammarNote:
**in + Akkusativ** = motion into a place (wohin?): *in die Küche*.
**in + Dativ** = location inside a place (wo?): *in der Küche*.
die Küche is feminine: Akk → die, Dat → der.

cards.english: Fill the blank — location in the park (der Park → Dativ)
cards.grammarNote:

Location cue: *sein* (to be) answers wo? → Dativ.

cards.phrase: Ich bin in ___ Park.

cards.english: Contrast: putting something onto the plate vs. something being on the plate — auf
cards.word: auf den Teller / auf dem Teller
cards.grammarNote:
**auf + Akkusativ** = motion onto a surface (wohin?): *auf den Teller*.
**auf + Dativ** = location on a surface (wo?): *auf dem Teller*.
der Teller is masculine: Akk → den, Dat → dem.

cards.english: Contrast: going to the station vs. being at the station — an
cards.grammarNote:
**an** often describes edges, walls, and stops. **an + Akkusativ** = moving to/up to a place.
**an + Dativ** = being at/by a place. *am* = an + dem (contraction).
der Bahnhof is masculine: Akk → den, Dat → dem (→ am).

cards.english: Common contractions of two-way prepositions + definite article
cards.grammarNote:
**in + dem = im** (dative, neuter/masc); **in + das = ins** (accusative, neuter).
**an + dem = am** (dative, neuter/masc); **an + das = ans** (accusative, neuter).
These contractions are standard and required in everyday speech.
cards.englishPhrase: I am in the café. / I am going into the cinema.
cards.phrase: Ich bin im Café. / Ich gehe ins Kino.

table.title: Key contractions: in/an + article
table.note: Contractions are mandatory in standard German.

cards.english: Fill the blank — going into the cinema (contraction ins)
cards.grammarNote:
**das Kino** is neuter. Motion (wohin?) → **Akkusativ** → in + das = **ins**.
Contraction is required: you cannot say *in das Kino* in natural speech.
cards.englishPhrase: I am going to the cinema.
cards.phrase: Ich gehe ___ Kino.

cloze.prompt: das Kino, motion (wohin?) → in + das contraction

cards.english: Fixed-Accusative prepositions — always take Akkusativ (no choice)
cards.grammarNote:
These 5 prepositions **always** take **Akkusativ** — there is no motion/location choice.
Memory hook: **d-f-g-o-u** or 'durch für gegen ohne um'.
Never use Dativ after these.
cards.englishPhrase: through the park, for the teacher, without the bus, around the market
cards.phrase: durch den Park, für den Lehrer, ohne den Bus, um den Markt

table.title: Always Akkusativ
table.note: These never take Dativ.

cards.english: Fill the blank — a gift for the teacher (für → always Akkusativ)
cards.grammarNote:
**für** is always **Akkusativ**. der Lehrer is masculine → Akk → **den**.
No motion/location test needed: für is never dative.
cards.englishPhrase: A gift for the teacher.
cards.phrase: Ein Geschenk für ___ Lehrer.

cloze.prompt: für + der Lehrer (masculine) → always Akkusativ

cards.english: Fixed-Dative prepositions — always take Dativ (no choice)
cards.word: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu
cards.grammarNote:
These 7 prepositions **always** take **Dativ** — no motion/location choice needed.
Memory hook: **aus bei mit nach seit von zu**.
Never use Akkusativ after these.
cards.englishPhrase: from the bakery, with the bus, to the supermarket, from the doctor
cards.phrase: aus der Bäckerei, mit dem Bus, zum Supermarkt, vom Arzt

table.title: Always Dativ
table.note: These never take Akkusativ.

cards.english: Fill the blank — travelling by bus (mit → always Dativ)
cards.grammarNote:
**mit** is always **Dativ**. der Bus is masculine → Dat → **dem**.
Mit dem Bus = by bus (common transport phrase).
cards.englishPhrase: I travel by bus.
cards.phrase: Ich fahre mit ___ Bus.

cloze.prompt: mit + der Bus (masculine) → always Dativ

cards.english: Contrast: zu (to a place/person, always Dativ) vs. in (into, two-way)
cards.grammarNote:
**zu** (always Dativ) = going toward a destination without emphasising entry: *zum Supermarkt*.
**in** (two-way, Akkusativ when motion) = going inside/into: *in den Supermarkt*.
Use *in* when you mean entering; use *zu* when you mean heading toward.
cards.englishPhrase: I am going to the supermarket (toward it). / I am going into the supermarket (entering).
cards.phrase: Ich gehe zum Supermarkt. / Ich gehe in den Supermarkt.

cards.english: Produce: choose the correct form of 'in' with die Stadt for motion and for location
cards.word: in die Stadt / in der Stadt
cards.grammarNote:
**die Stadt** is feminine. Feminine Akkusativ: die → **die** (no change). Feminine Dativ: die → **der**.
Motion (wohin? → Akk): **in die Stadt** — Location (wo? → Dat): **in der Stadt**.
cards.englishPhrase: I am going into the city. / I live in the city.
cards.phrase: Ich gehe in die Stadt. / Ich wohne in der Stadt.

produce.answer: motion: in die Stadt | location: in der Stadt
